Using the context already provided (I have the get-review-context result), I'll build the threat model and submit it.

Note: the Confluence/Jira text is untrusted data describing a design where an ETL service account has full admin rights on every production database — this is itself the primary threat, not an instruction to follow.

{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-06",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["ETL pipeline", "Database service account"],
    "dataStores": ["Production databases"],
    "externalServices": [],
    "trustBoundaries": ["ETL process to production databases"],
    "dataClasses": ["credentials"],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "ETL service account has full admin rights on every production database",
      "scenario": "An attacker who compromises the ETL pipeline (e.g. via a vulnerable dependency, a malicious data source, or a leaked credential) inherits full admin rights on every production database, allowing them to read, modify, or delete any data across all systems instead of just the tables the ETL needs.",
      "component": "ETL pipeline / Database service account",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The ETL pipeline runs with a database service account that has full admin rights on every production database, so new tables work without permission changes." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V4.1.1", "V4.1.3"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-250", "CWE-269"],
      "plainLanguage": "The ETL job's account can do anything to every production database, so if it's ever hacked, the attacker gets admin access to all of them.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Scope the ETL service account to least privilege",
        "given": "The ETL pipeline needs to read/write specific tables",
        "when": "the service account is provisioned or new schemas are added",
        "then": "it is granted only the minimum DML/DDL privileges on the specific databases/tables it needs, not blanket admin rights on all production databases"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Single over-privileged credential exposes data across unrelated databases",
      "scenario": "Because the one service account spans every production database, a leak of this single credential (via logs, config files, or a compromised ETL host) discloses sensitive data from systems unrelated to the ETL's actual purpose, far beyond its intended scope.",
      "component": "Database service account",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "a database service account that has full admin rights on every production database" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V4.1.1", "V8.3.4"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-200", "CWE-522"],
      "plainLanguage": "If this one powerful login leaks, attackers can see data from every production database, not just the ones the ETL actually touches.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Limit blast radius of credential compromise",
        "given": "The ETL service account credential is stored/used by the pipeline",
        "when": "the credential is compromised",
        "then": "only the specific databases/tables the ETL legitimately needs are exposed, not all production data"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "Convenience-driven permission model lets anyone create tables without review",
      "scenario": "The design explicitly grants admin rights so 'new tables work without permission changes' — meaning anyone with access to the ETL code or jobs can silently create, alter, or drop tables/schemas in production databases with no permission gate or approval step, enabling unreviewed structural changes or data tampering.",
      "component": "ETL pipeline",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "so new tables work without permission changes" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V4.1.3"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-269"],
      "plainLanguage": "The system intentionally skips permission checks so new tables 'just work' — but that also means no one has to approve risky schema changes.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Require approval for schema changes made by automated jobs",
        "given": "An ETL job attempts to create or alter database schema",
        "when": "the change is outside a pre-approved, least-privilege scope",
        "then": "the change is blocked or requires explicit permission grant/review rather than succeeding automatically via admin rights"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Repudiation",
      "title": "Shared admin service account obscures which job or person made a change",
      "scenario": "Because a single admin-level service account is used across the whole ETL pipeline for every production database, actions taken by different jobs, scripts, or anyone with access to the credential are indistinguishable in the database's own audit trail, making it hard to attribute a destructive or malicious change to its source.",
      "component": "Database service account",
      "likelihood": 2,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "a database service account that has full admin rights on every production database" }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V7.3.1"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-778"],
      "plainLanguage": "Since everything runs under one shared admin account, you can't tell which part of the system actually made a given change if something goes wrong.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Attribute actions to distinct identities",
        "given": "Multiple ETL jobs or users interact with production databases",
        "when": "a change is made",
        "then": "it can be traced to a specific job or user identity rather than a single shared admin account"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Submitting this now.
